objects.title: Temple of Portunus
objects.note: The standing temple, modelled in the catalogue. Footprint is the present-day OpenStreetMap outline; the model itself is drawn from a historic plan (see its own evidence card).

objects.title: Temple of Hercules Victor
objects.note: The standing round temple, modelled in the catalogue. Footprint is the present-day OpenStreetMap outline; its original roof is lost.

objects.title: Pons Aemilius
objects.note: Four piers as Lanciani drew them (the Ponte Rotto pier at E -121.4 m is also fixed by the surviving arch outline at E -134.5 to -105.6 m); stone, seven spans (Wikipedia). The three east piers are spaced evenly to the ancient bank he surveyed; the deck width and arch profile are guessed.

objects.title: River quay · Portus Tiberinus frontage
objects.note: A stone-faced river wall with steps, set along the bank as Lanciani's plate shows it before the embankments (an approximation of the ancient shore; here no wall is drawn). That Rome's river harbour had built quays is likely, but no source here records this stretch.

objects.title: Tiber quay wall · Forum Boarium frontage
objects.snap: Lanciani marks this wall (excavated in the 19th century) but does not date it, so it is taken as standing at AD 100; river walls here were Republican to imperial and were repaired, not replaced.
objects.note: A stone river wall along the Forum Boarium, on the line Lanciani drew as the excavated riverfront ("RIPA"), 30 to 17 m east of today's bank. Its position is read from his plate to about 3-5 m; its height, facing and steps are guessed.

objects.title: River quay · south of the Forum Boarium
objects.note: A stone-faced river wall with steps, set along the bank as Lanciani's plate shows it before the embankments (an approximation of the ancient shore; here no wall is drawn). That Rome's river harbour had built quays is likely, but no source here records this stretch.

objects.title: Riverside road
objects.note: A road running along the quay behind the river wall. Its line is today's east bank offset inland; nothing records it, so it is a guess.

objects.title: Road from the bridge to the Velabrum
objects.note: Platner records a road leading from the bridge across the Forum Boarium towards the Velabrum. The route is bent here to pass north of the Temple of Portunus; its exact line is a guess.

objects.title: Vicus Tuscus · Forum end
objects.note: The line OpenStreetMap maps for the Vicus Tuscus at its Forum end (Pleiades locates it to about 20 m). Width and paving are guessed.

objects.title: Vicus Tuscus · through the Velabrum to the market
objects.note: Pleiades and Wikipedia say the street ran from the Forum along the western flank of the Palatine, through the Velabrum, to the Forum Boarium (processions went this way to the Circus). Its exact line is guessed along today's Via di San Teodoro and Via del Velabro, which lie in the same valley.

objects.title: Vicus Iugarius · Forum end
objects.note: The line OpenStreetMap maps for the Vicus Iugarius near the Forum. Pleiades says it led from the Forum to the Porta Carmentalis. Width and paving are guessed.

objects.title: Vicus Iugarius · foot of the Capitoline to the market
objects.note: Platner names the Vicus Iugarius as a route into the Forum Boarium and Pleiades has it leaving by the Porta Carmentalis. Its line along the foot of the Capitoline is guessed from today's Via della Consolazione and Via del Velabro.

objects.title: Clivus Victoriae
objects.note: The steep street up the Palatine, on the line OpenStreetMap maps for it (Pleiades locates it to about 20 m). Width and paving are guessed.

objects.title: Road from the market to the Circus Maximus
objects.note: The Forum Boarium opened towards the starting gates of the Circus Maximus (Platner, Wikipedia). The road is likely; its line is guessed along today's Via dei Cerchi.

objects.title: Road west of the bridge into Trastevere
objects.note: The Pons Aemilius led over the river to the west bank. A road continuing from the bridge is likely; its line and width are guessed.

objects.title: Theatre of Marcellus
objects.note: Position, radius (61.1 m to the outer arcade, as the plate reads; Wikipedia gives a diameter of 111 m) and the half-ring plan are from Lanciani's plate, which draws the surviving arcade and the lost cavea; finished 13 BC (Wikipedia). The arcades' three storeys, the seating bowl and the stage building are massing, guessed.

objects.title: Temple of Janus · Forum Holitorium
objects.snap: Founded in the First Punic War and restored in AD 17 (Wikipedia); the plan is as Lanciani drew its remains, so it stood in AD 100.
objects.note: One of the three republican temples on the Forum Holitorium (vegetable market), facing east. Its place, size and tilt are read from Lanciani's plate (about 3-5 m), the number of columns from Wikipedia; its column order, heights, podium and roof are massing, guessed. Columns of the Spes and Juno temples still stand in San Nicola in Carcere.

objects.title: Temple of Juno Sospita · Forum Holitorium
objects.snap: Founded about 195 BC and rebuilt in 90 BC (Wikipedia); the plan is as Lanciani drew its remains, so it stood in AD 100.
objects.note: One of the three republican temples on the Forum Holitorium (vegetable market), facing east. Its place, size and tilt are read from Lanciani's plate (about 3-5 m), the number of columns from Wikipedia; its column order, heights, podium and roof are massing, guessed. Columns of the Spes and Juno temples still stand in San Nicola in Carcere.

objects.title: Temple of Spes · Forum Holitorium
objects.snap: Founded in the First Punic War, rebuilt after the fire of 213 BC and restored in AD 17 (Wikipedia); the plan is as Lanciani drew its remains, so it stood in AD 100.
objects.note: One of the three republican temples on the Forum Holitorium (vegetable market), facing east. Its place, size and tilt are read from Lanciani's plate (about 3-5 m), the number of columns from Wikipedia; its column order, heights, podium and roof are massing, guessed. Columns of the Spes and Juno temples still stand in San Nicola in Carcere.

objects.title: Porticus Minucia (as Lanciani placed it) · colonnaded hall
objects.snap: Lanciani draws the piers as found and names them Porticus Minucia; the name and date are his identification, not secure, so it is shown within a window of 50 years around AD 100.
objects.note: A hall of rows of piers between two long walls, about 85 by 33 m, placed where Lanciani drew its remains; the label Porticus Minucia is his identification and later scholars place the porticoes of that name elsewhere. Pier spacing, heights and the roof are guessed.

objects.title: Pons Fabricius · east bank to Tiber Island
objects.note: The bridge to the island from the Forum Holitorium side, with two arches and a central pier as Lanciani draws it (it still stands). Its ends are read from his plate to about 3-5 m; the deck width, parapets and arch profile are guessed.
objects.snap: Dated 62 BC by its inscription, and still in use; it stood in AD 100 as drawn.

objects.title: Pons Cestius · Tiber Island to Trastevere
objects.note: The bridge from the island to the west bank, three spans as Lanciani draws the piers. Its line is read from his plate to about 3-5 m; the span lengths, deck width and arch profile are guessed. The present bridge dates from 1892; the Roman one was rebuilt in AD 370.
objects.snap: Built about 46 BC and rebuilt in AD 370; the earlier bridge is shown, on the line Lanciani gives.

objects.title: Temple of Aesculapius · Tiber Island
objects.snap: A temple of the god stood on the island from the 3rd century BC; the remains Lanciani drew are taken as the building of AD 100.
objects.note: The island's temple of the healing god, where Lanciani labels it (T. AESCVLAPI, with excavated remains). Its place is read from his plate to about 3-5 m; its orientation, size, column count, order and heights are guessed.

objects.title: Circus Maximus
objects.note: The long axis and extent are fitted to the OpenStreetMap outline of the excavated site (596 m long); the track is 118 m wide and the whole circus about 621 m long (Wikipedia). Seating, the central barrier with Augustus's obelisk, the starting gates and the outer arcade are massing only: the depth of the stands, tier heights and the 24 m outer wall are guessed. Trajan's stone rebuilding began just after AD 100.

objects.title: Domus Flavia · imperial palace (public wing)
objects.note: Position and size fitted to the surviving walls OpenStreetMap maps (152 by 100 m); completed about AD 92 by Domitian (Pleiades, Wikipedia). Wall height (the rooms about 18 m; the great hall over 30 m, with a 30.6 m span) follows Wikipedia. The courtyard, the hall's place and every roof and facade are massing, not a reconstruction.

objects.title: Domus Augustana · imperial palace (residential wing)
objects.note: Position and size fitted to the surviving walls OpenStreetMap maps (225 by 86 m); the central block of Domitian's palace, finished about AD 92, with two peristyles and a great curved exedra facing the Circus Maximus (Wikipedia). Heights, the courts and the exedra's size are massing, guessed.

objects.title: Domus Tiberiana · imperial palace (north-west corner of the Palatine)
objects.note: The platform at the north-west corner of the hill, fitted to the walls OpenStreetMap maps (220 by 120 m); Wikipedia gives about 150 by 120 m and arcaded supports on the north slope, rebuilt under Domitian. Its height and courtyard are massing, guessed.

objects.title: Basalt-paved street to the Forum Holitorium
objects.note: A broad street paved with polygonal basalt blocks, found by excavation in 1873 and drawn by Lanciani running from the Forum Holitorium (the Porta Carmentalis end) down to the Forum Boarium; he took it for the Vicus Iugarius, which is likely but not certain. Its line is read from his plate to about 3-5 m; its width follows the plate, its kerbs and gutters are guessed.
objects.snap: The paving is undated on Lanciani's plate; basalt-paved city streets are common from the Republic on, so it is taken as laid by AD 100.

objects.title: Paved cross street west of the basalt street
objects.note: A second paved band, found in 1873 and drawn by Lanciani crossing the basalt street towards the river. Its line and width are read from his plate; what it was (a street or the front of a building) is not stated, so a street is assumed.
objects.snap: Undated on the plate; taken as in place by AD 100 with the street it crosses.

objects.title: Cloaca Maxima · course to the river
objects.note: The great drain, on the course Lanciani drew from the river wall, where it enters between the temples and the bank, east to a bend and on towards the Velabrum. In the market it ran vaulted and underground, so it is shown on the map only; its width is drawn from the plate and its vault is not modelled.

objects.title: Cloaca Circi Maximi · drain from the circus
objects.note: The channel Lanciani marks from the Circus Maximus valley to the river, passing the Schola Graeca. Its course is read from his plate to about 3-5 m; it was vaulted where it crossed the market, so it is shown on the map only.

objects.title: Statio Annonae · grain-supply office and colonnaded hall
objects.snap: Lanciani draws the Statio Annonae (found 1778 and later) on the site where Santa Maria in Cosmedin was later built into it. No source here dates the hall exactly; it belongs to the imperial grain service, so it is shown from about AD 100 within a window of 50 years either way.
objects.note: The grain office and its colonnaded hall, placed on the 53 by 26 m site Lanciani gives it beside the Schola Graeca and the Ara Maxima. Its position and size follow his plan; its walls, roof and heights are massing, guessed.

objects.title: Timber landing stage 1
objects.note: A timber landing stage for the river harbour. The Portus Tiberinus is recorded only as a point about 1 km wide and as in use to at least AD 96; the stages and their spacing are guessed.

objects.title: Moored river barge 1
objects.note: A river barge of the kind that brought goods upstream from Ostia, towed by men on the bank (Italian Wikipedia). Size, cargo and mooring are guessed.

objects.title: Forum Boarium · open paved square
objects.note: The cattle market was an open public space (Platner, Wikipedia). The present-day site outline is widened slightly here to give an open square; the true ancient extent is not recorded, and its surface (paving) is a guess.

objects.title: Ara Maxima of Hercules
objects.note: Placed at Pleiades' derived point for the altar; its foundations are tentatively a tuff platform in the crypt of Santa Maria in Cosmedin. Size, steps and the altar block are guessed.

objects.title: Cattle pen 1
objects.note: A timber-railed pen for the cattle market. The market is documented; pens, their number and their place are guessed.

insula.title: Insula · shops below, flats above
insula.note: A multi-storey block of flats with shops (tabernae) along the ground floor, the usual form in Roman streets (Wikipedia, Insula). Heights stay under the Roman limit of about 17.75 m. That a block stood here, and its size and height, are guesses.

flats.title: Block of flats (insula)
flats.note: A multi-storey block of flats, typical of the dense streets and courtyards of Roman districts (Wikipedia, Insula). Heights stay under the Roman limit of about 17.75 m. That a block stood here, and its size, are guesses.

shop.title: Shop-house (taberna) with rooms above
shop.note: A shop with a wide opening at street level and rooms above, the usual form in Roman streets (Wikipedia, Insula). That a shop stood here is a guess; so are its size and height.

warehouse.title: Riverside warehouse (horreum)
warehouse.note: A two-storey warehouse with thick walls and few, high windows (Wikipedia, Horrea). Riverside storage near the harbour is likely; this building's place and size are guessed.

lane.title: Back lane
lane.note: A narrow lane between blocks, the usual fine grain of Roman districts (Wikipedia, Insula). That a lane ran here, and its width, are guesses; the lines are laid out by the generator, not recorded.
